facts.title: Last Natural Element Found
facts.text: Francium was the last element discovered in nature, identified in 1939 by Marguerite Perey at the Curie Institute in Paris. She spotted it while purifying a sample of actinium and noticed an unexpected radioactive decay product. It was the final element on the periodic table to be found in a natural source rather than created artificially in a lab.

facts.title: Named For France
facts.text: Marguerite Perey named the element after her home country, France, giving it the symbol Fr. She originally proposed the name 'catium' for its strongly cation-forming nature, but colleagues worried it sounded too much like 'cat' in English. Perey later became the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences in 1962.

facts.title: Vanishingly Rare On Earth
facts.text: Francium is the second-rarest naturally occurring element, after astatine. Scientists estimate that at any given moment the entire Earth's crust contains only about 20 to 30 grams of it, scattered as fleeting atoms inside uranium and thorium minerals. It forms continuously as a decay product but vanishes almost as fast as it appears.

facts.title: A Fleeting Half-Life
facts.text: Francium's most stable isotope, francium-223, has a half-life of only about 22 minutes, and every other isotope decays even faster. This extreme instability means no one has ever assembled a visible, weighable lump of the metal. Any sample large enough to see would generate so much heat from its own radioactivity that it would instantly vaporize itself.

facts.title: The Heaviest Alkali Metal
facts.text: Francium sits at the bottom of Group 1, making it the heaviest of the alkali metals below lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium. Based on periodic trends, it should be the most reactive of them all and would react violently with water. Because so few atoms have ever existed at once, this dramatic reaction has never actually been observed directly.

facts.title: Trapped By Lasers
facts.text: In 1995, physicists at Stony Brook University used magneto-optical traps and laser cooling to hold clouds of about 10,000 francium atoms suspended in a vacuum. This let them study francium's light spectrum without ever needing a solid sample. The glowing trapped atoms were even photographed, producing some of the only real images of francium's behavior.

facts.title: A Probe For Fundamental Physics
facts.text: Francium's heavy nucleus and single outer electron make it a prized testing ground for studying the weak nuclear force and parity violation. Researchers at facilities like TRIUMF in Canada produce francium atoms specifically to hunt for tiny deviations from the Standard Model of particle physics. Its simple structure plus large size amplifies subtle effects that are nearly impossible to measure in lighter atoms.

facts.title: Made To Order In Accelerators
facts.text: Because natural francium is so scarce, scientists manufacture it by bombarding gold or thorium targets with beams of oxygen or proton ions in particle accelerators. This approach can produce up to roughly a million francium atoms per second for experiments. Even at that rate, the atoms decay continuously, so they must be studied the instant they are created.

facts.title: No Biological Role
facts.text: Francium has no known function in any living organism, and because it is both incredibly rare and intensely radioactive, it plays no part in biology or nutrition. Living things never encounter meaningful amounts of it. Any practical danger comes purely from its radioactivity rather than chemical toxicity, but no realistic exposure scenario exists outside a research lab.

facts.title: Once Mistaken For New Elements
facts.text: Before Perey's confirmation, francium was the subject of several false claims and placeholder names, including 'eka-caesium,' 'virginium' and 'moldavium.' Dmitri Mendeleev had predicted the missing element decades earlier, foreseeing a heavy alkali metal beneath caesium. It took until 1939 for genuine, reproducible evidence to settle the long search for element 87.
